findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes
findings.body: All four background goroutines (Create l.51, Delete l.110, Update l.135, DeleteCollection l.163) build their timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context. A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is cancelled, and the apiserver cancels the request context the moment the handler returns — which happens immediately after `return created, err`. So in practice the legacy write will frequently (often always, for fast handlers) be aborted with `context.Canceled` before or during execution, which silently defeats the whole point of mode 3 (writing a safety copy to legacy). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving auth/user values) as the parent before applying the timeout, so the write survives the request lifecycle.

findings.title: Errors from the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged
findings.body: In Create (l.55-56), Delete (l.112-113), Update (l.139-140) and DeleteCollection (l.165-166) the error returned by the legacy storage is only fed into a duration histogram and then dropped. The previous implementation logged these failures. Since mode 3 reads exclusively from unified storage, a failing legacy write produces a silent divergence between the two stores with no diagnostic trail (no object name, no error message), making it impossible to reconcile later. Log the error with the object identity (and the timeout cause when the ctx expired).

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric
findings.body: In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The same mistake exists in `Update` (l.129). This attributes unified-storage latency/failures to the legacy histogram, so the storage histogram never records any failures and the legacy histogram is polluted with samples for an operation legacy never performed. Both should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

findings.title: Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label (unbounded cardinality)
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each deleted object therefore creates a new time series in the duration histogram, which is an unbounded-cardinality label and will blow up the Prometheus registry/scrape payload on any workload that deletes many objects. It also makes the metric unusable for per-kind aggregation. Should be `options.Kind`.

findings.title: DeleteCollection goroutine records legacy latency as storage latency
findings.body: Inside the async goroutine of `DeleteCollection` the legacy call's duration is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` using `startLegacy`. This means the legacy DeleteCollection duration/errors appear under the unified-storage metric, double-counting storage samples for the same request and leaving the legacy metric with no data for delete-collection. Should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`.

findings.title: Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object actually persisted in storage
findings.body: The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy received exactly the object that was written to unified storage. Now the raw `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update`, so legacy recomputes the updated object from *its own* stored copy. For PATCH/Apply requests, or when the client sent a resourceVersion precondition (the RV now belongs to unified storage, not legacy), this either fails with a conflict or writes a different object than the one in unified storage, producing a silent divergence between the two stores. Pass the storage result through `updateWrapper` as before.

findings.title: Request-scoped object and validation callbacks are used from a goroutine after the request completed
findings.body: The goroutines pass the caller-owned `obj` (Create, l.55) and the request's `createValidation`/`updateValidation`/`deleteValidation` funcs (l.55, 112, 139, 165) into the legacy store after the handler has returned. `obj` has already been mutated in place by the unified-storage create path and is still reachable from the handler, and the validation closures run admission, which writes audit annotations onto the request's audit event — an event the audit backend may be serializing concurrently once the request finished. This is a real data race / mutation-after-response hazard. Deep-copy the object before handing it to the goroutine and avoid re-running request-scoped validation/admission on the async path.

findings.title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` built one line above with name/kind/method values. Any downstream code that pulls the logger from the context (`klog.FromContext`) loses the request identifying fields for deletes only, making delete failures hard to correlate. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

findings.title: Tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: Every mode 3 test only asserts on the value returned from the unified store; no test waits for or asserts that `Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` was invoked (e.g. via `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` after synchronization). Because the legacy goroutine is fire-and-forget, the core behaviour added by this PR — the safety write to legacy — is completely untested, and the regression described above (the goroutine's context being cancelled with the request) would not be caught. The goroutines also outlive the subtest, so the mock is exercised after the test function returns, which makes any future expectation mismatch surface as a panic in a background goroutine rather than a test failure.

findings.title: Storage-failure test case is configured through setupLegacyFn and only works because both mocks share one mock.Mock
findings.body: In the "error when creating object in the unified store fails" case the failing `Create` expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` while `setupStorageFn` is nil. It only produces the expected error because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` are constructed around the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage call matches the legacy expectation. The test therefore cannot distinguish a legacy failure from a storage failure and is misleading for anyone adding cases later; register the expectation on the storage setup function.

findings.title: go.work.sum contains a duplicated entry and unrelated dependency hashes
findings.body: The added block re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` which already exists two lines above, and adds hashes for modules unrelated to this change (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel versions). This looks like a locally dirty workspace file committed by accident rather than a regenerated one; it will churn/conflict on the next `go work sync`. Regenerate the file or drop these lines from the PR.
